holdings.quote: To reiterate, the question is whether the ground on which the RAD decided the appeal is a new issue in the sense that it is legally and factually distinct from the grounds of appeal advanced and cannot reasonably be said to stem from the issues as framed by the respondents (the respondents being the only party to the appeal for the purpose of this part of the analysis).
holdings.statement: The Mian test asks whether the ground on which the RAD decided the appeal is a new issue that is legally and factually distinct from the grounds of appeal advanced and cannot reasonably be said to stem from the issues as framed by the respondents.

holdings.quote: Only if this question is answered affirmatively will it have been a breach of the requirements of procedural fairness for the RAD to decide the appeal on the basis that it did without first providing the Minister an opportunity to be heard in relation to it.
holdings.statement: If the ground is a new issue, it is a breach of procedural fairness for the RAD to decide the appeal on that basis without first giving the Minister an opportunity to be heard.

holdings.quote: Applying this test, I have concluded that the sur place claim is a new issue and, as a result, the RAD was required to give notice to the Minister (and, of course, to the respondents) that it could be considered in deciding the appeal and, further, that all parties should have had an opportunity to address this issue before the appeal was decided.
holdings.statement: The sur place claim is a new issue, so the RAD was required to give notice to the Minister and the respondents and allow them to address it before deciding the appeal.

holdings.quote: The sur place claims are legally and factually distinct from the grounds of appeal related to the threshold issue of identity and also from the new evidence tendered by the respondents. Moreover, they cannot reasonably be said to stem from the issues as framed by the respondents in their appeal.
holdings.statement: The sur place claims are legally and factually distinct from the grounds of appeal related to identity and the new evidence tendered by the respondents, and do not stem from the issues framed by the respondents in their appeal.

holdings.quote: In these circumstances, the Minister can fairly be said to have been taken by surprise that the appeal was decided on the ground that it was.
holdings.statement: The Minister was taken by surprise that the appeal was decided on the sur place claim ground.

holdings.quote: The important point is that these claims were not – indeed, could not be – part of the grounds of appeal as they were framed by the respondents.
holdings.statement: The sur place claims could not be part of the grounds of appeal as framed by the respondents.

holdings.quote: As I have explained above, in deciding an appeal the RAD has jurisdiction to consider issues the RPD did not address in its decision and, further, the RAD is not limited to considering the issues raised on appeal.
holdings.statement: The RAD has jurisdiction to consider issues not addressed by the RPD and is not limited to issues raised on appeal.

holdings.quote: However, when, as happened here, the case has materially shifted away from the RPD’s decision and the appeal as it was framed by the respondents, the RAD breached the requirements of procedural fairness by deciding the appeal on the basis on which it did without first giving the Minister notice that a new issue was in play and an opportunity to be heard.
holdings.statement: When the case materially shifts away from the RPD’s decision and the appeal as framed by the respondents, the RAD breaches procedural fairness by deciding on that new basis without giving the Minister notice and an opportunity to be heard.

holdings.quote: Finally, I am satisfied that this breach of the requirements of procedural fairness warrants setting aside the RAD’s decision.
holdings.statement: The breach of procedural fairness by the RAD warrants setting aside its decision.

holdings.quote: Regrettably, because of how the RAD proceeded, this did not happen.
holdings.statement: Because the RAD proceeded without proper notice and opportunity to be heard, the procedural fairness required by Baker was not met.

holdings.quote: For these reasons, the Minister’s application for judicial review is allowed.
holdings.statement: The Minister's application for judicial review is allowed.

holdings.quote: The decision of the Refugee Appeal Division dated January 21, 2020, is set aside and the matter is remitted for redetermination by a different decision maker.
holdings.statement: The decision of the Refugee Appeal Division dated January 21, 2020, is set aside and the matter is remitted for redetermination by a different decision maker.

holdings.quote: For greater certainty, unless the Minister presents new evidence calling into question the personal identities of the respondents, the RAD shall proceed on the basis that the personal identities of the respondents are established.
holdings.statement: Unless the Minister presents new evidence calling into question the personal identities of the respondents, the RAD shall proceed on the basis that the personal identities of the respondents are established.

holdings.quote: The parties did not propose any serious questions of general importance for certification under paragraph 74(d) of the IRPA.
holdings.statement: The parties did not propose any serious questions of general importance for certification under paragraph 74(d) of the IRPA.

holdings.quote: I agree that none arise.
holdings.statement: No serious questions of general importance arise for certification under paragraph 74(d) of the IRPA.

rebuttals.quote: I do not agree. It is well-established that a decision maker is not required to address every argument that arises on the record (Vavilov at para 91, citing Newfoundland and Labrador Nurses’ Union v Newfoundland and Labrador (Treasury Board), 2011 SCC 62, [2011] 3 SCR 708, at para 16). This latitude is especially apt when, as is the case here, the arguments in question were not made on the appeal to the RAD but only earlier in the process, to the RPD. The RPD did not adopt those arguments in its reasons and, as a result, they were not addressed in the respondents’ submissions to the RAD. As the Supreme Court observes in Vavilov, the review of an administrative decision “can be divorced neither from the institutional context in which the decision was made nor from the history of the proceedings” (at para 91).
rebuttals.court_answer: The court disagrees, noting that a decision maker is not required to address every argument on the record, especially those not raised on appeal to the RAD but only before the RPD, and that the review must consider the institutional context and history of proceedings.

rebuttals.quote: According to the respondents, it is only the parties to an appeal who would be entitled to notice in any event and, because he did not intervene, the Minister was not a party to the appeal. Thus, I cannot agree with the respondents that, having opted not to intervene after receiving their Record, the Minister had no right to notice of a subsequent development affecting the determination of the appeal and the respondents’ claims for protection.
rebuttals.court_answer: The respondents' argument that the Minister had no right to notice after opting not to intervene is rejected because the Minister retains procedural fairness rights.

authorities.quote: That this is the appropriate standard of review has been reinforced by Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65. Reasonableness is now the presumptive standard of review for administrative decisions, subject to specific exceptions “only where required by a clear indication of legislative intent or by the rule of law” (Vavilov at para 10). There is no basis for derogating from this presumption here.
authorities.authority: The reasonableness standard of review for administrative decisions is reinforced by Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65, which establishes reasonableness as the presumptive standard subject to specific exceptions.

authorities.quote: Justice Hughes expressed this exception to the general rule as follows in Husian v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 FC 684 at para 10: “The point is that if the RAD chooses to take a frolic and venture into the record to make further substantive findings, it should give some sort of notice to the parties and give them an opportunity to make submissions.”
authorities.authority: Justice Hughes in Husian v Canada stated that if the RAD makes further substantive findings, it should give notice to the parties and an opportunity to make submissions.

authorities.quote: The issue in Mian was what should happen as a matter of procedural fairness when an appeal court raises an issue that was not raised by the parties. If the appellate court raises a new issue, fairness to the adversarial process requires the court to provide the parties with notice and an opportunity to respond to it: Mian, at para. 30.
authorities.authority: The test in R v Mian balances the adversarial process and the appellate court's duty to ensure justice, requiring notice and opportunity to respond if a new issue is raised.

authorities.quote: However, where the appellate court raises an issue that is not “new” but rather is rooted in or forms a component of the issues raised by the parties, Mian gives appellate courts a discretion to determine whether notice and submissions are warranted: para. 33.
authorities.authority: Where the appellate court raises an issue not new but rooted in or forming a component of the issues raised by the parties, the court has discretion whether notice and submissions are warranted.

authorities.quote: As the Supreme Court of Canada held in Baker (at para 22), “the purpose of the participatory rights contained within the duty of procedural fairness is to ensure that administrative decisions are made using a fair and open procedure, appropriate to the decision being made and its statutory, institutional, and social context, with an opportunity for those affected by the decision to put forward their views and evidence fully and have them considered by the decision-maker.”
authorities.authority: The Supreme Court of Canada in Baker held that procedural fairness ensures decisions are made with a fair and open procedure allowing affected parties to fully present their views and evidence.

left_open.quote: (The Minister may well also have the right to present evidence on the new issue; however, since the Minister’s complaint here is limited to the denial of the right to make submissions on the basis of the record before the RPD, I leave this question open.)
left_open.issue: Whether the Minister has the right to present evidence on the new issue is left open as the Minister's complaint is limited to denial of the right to make submissions on the record before the RPD.
left_open.reason: Minister's right to present evidence left open

left_open.quote: (How such notice should be given is, in the first instance, for the RAD to determine but it may find the suggestions in Mian at paragraphs 53 to 60 of assistance.)
left_open.issue: How the RAD should give notice of a new issue is for the RAD to determine, but it may consider suggestions in Mian paragraphs 53 to 60.
left_open.reason: Left to RAD to determine how to give notice.

left_open.quote: As I have already stated, it is not necessary to address this issue.
left_open.issue: It is not necessary to address the reasonableness of RAD's refugee determination.
